Wednesday, 8 pm. Today's review meeting was in Hindi and English mixed, as always. Gautam, who joined last month from Chennai, sat with his notebook and a small line between his eyebrows. He understood the English, but Hindi asides went fast.
So I decided, whenever I made a key point, I would say it twice: once in Hindi and once in English. "Delivery moves to Tuesday. Delivery Mangalvar ko hogi." Nobody mocked it. Ritu even nodded.
After the meeting Gautam came over. "Thanks for saying it twice. I got all of it today," he said quietly.
It cost me maybe thirty seconds. I'm keeping the habit.
— Saurabh

qa.q: What day did Saurabh say the delivery would move to?
qa.a: Saurabh said delivery moves to Tuesday.

qa.q: What might Gautam have been feeling during the meeting before Saurabh started repeating?
qa.a: Gautam was probably anxious and a little left out, since the line between the eyebrows and the notebook show effort to follow. Fast Hindi asides were hard to catch.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do that included Gautam without slowing the meeting much?
qa.a: Saurabh said each key point twice, once in Hindi and once in English. It cost about thirty seconds and nobody objected.

qa.q: What is it like for Gautam to get the key points in both languages?
qa.a: Gautam feels relieved and respected, saying "I got all of it today". Being included makes joining the discussion easier.

grounding: In a mixed-language meeting, a speaker repeats key points in both languages so a less fluent member is not left out.

Team chat, after the 4 pm meeting
Vishal: Quick recap for everyone. English first, Hindi below.
Vishal: 1) Sample goes out Friday. 2) Ritu will call the vendor. 3) Next meeting Monday 11.
Vishal: Hindi mein: 1) Sample Friday ko jayega. 2) Ritu vendor ko call karegi. 3) Agla meeting Monday 11 baje.
Ritu: Thanks! I missed the middle part when everyone switched to Hindi. This helps 🙂
Vishal: Of course. Tell me anytime if I move too fast. Happy to repeat it.
Ritu: Will do. Same for you if my English gets fast!

qa.q: What time is the next meeting on Monday?
qa.a: The next meeting is Monday at 11.

qa.q: What did Vishal want when posting the recap in both languages?
qa.a: Vishal wanted nobody to be left out and wanted Ritu and others to feel able to say when it went too fast. The offer to repeat anything shows patient care.

qa.q: What did Vishal do after the meeting to help everyone follow?
qa.a: Vishal posted the recap in English first and then in Hindi, and invited Ritu to say if it went too fast. That included both language groups.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel about the recap, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Ritu felt relieved and grateful, saying the middle part was missed and that the recap helps. Offering to do the same for Vishal shows the goodwill.

grounding: After a mixed-language meeting, a speaker posts the key points in both languages so no one is left out.

passage:
In the village hall near Barpeta, twenty farmers sat on mats for the soil-testing meeting. Bidisha, from the district agriculture office, spoke in Assamese; most farmers nodded. But Karthik, the new soil scientist from Coimbatore, sat at the side, following nothing. And three women from the tea garden line spoke mainly Sadri and Hindi.
Bidisha noticed Karthik's pen hadn't moved and the women were whispering to each other.
She paused. "Let me repeat the main points in Hindi, so we're all together." She said it slowly: samples on Thursday, one bag per field, label with your name.
Karthik began writing. One of the women raised her hand and asked, in Hindi, whether the kitchen garden could be tested too.
"Good question," Bidisha said, and answered, then put it back into Assamese for the rest.
After the meeting Karthik said, "Thank you. I thought I'd have to ask you to repeat everything."

qa.q: When were the soil samples to be collected?
qa.a: The samples were on Thursday.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel before Bidisha switched to Hindi?
qa.a: Karthik likely felt lost and left out, sitting at the side following nothing, with his pen not moving.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Bidisha paused to repeat the key points slowly in the shared language, which brought Karthik and the women into the meeting and even drew out a new question.

qa.q: How might the tea garden women see Bidisha after the meeting?
qa.a: They likely feel respected and included, since they could ask about the kitchen garden and got a real answer.

grounding: In a mixed-language meeting, a speaker repeats key points in the shared language so no one is left out.

passage:
The startup in Lisbon held its Monday meeting in Portuguese, mostly. Chidi, who had joined from Lagos two months ago, understood about half, and he'd started nodding along to things he'd missed.
Lucia, the product lead, noticed him nodding a beat too late when the team decided to move the launch. She stopped.
"Sorry, quick switch. In English: the launch moves to the twelfth, Chidi's payment screen needs to be ready by the fifth, and we'll test on the eighth." She turned to the table. "From now on, I'll give the decisions in English at the end. Everyone okay with that?"
The others nodded. Chidi looked up. "Thank you. I would have missed the fifth."
"That's exactly why," Lucia said.
After the meeting, Chidi stayed back and asked her for the Portuguese word for "deadline", so he could say it next time himself.

qa.q: When did Chidi's payment screen need to be ready?
qa.a: Chidi's payment screen needed to be ready by the fifth.

qa.q: What was Chidi feeling as he nodded along in the meeting?
qa.a: Chidi felt lost and a bit embarrassed, nodding a beat too late to hide that he only understood about half.

qa.q: What small adjustment did Lucia make, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She repeated the key decisions in English and promised to do it every time, so no one misses a deadline because of language.

qa.q: What would change if Lucia had not noticed Chidi's nodding?
qa.a: Chidi might have missed the fifth and felt more shut out, and the team's launch could have slipped.

grounding: In a mixed-language meeting, a speaker repeats key points in the shared language so a less fluent colleague is not left out.

passage:
The nursing staff meeting at the Bengaluru hospital started, as usual, in fast Kannada. Gautam, the senior nurse in charge, ran through the week: a new infection-control checklist, a change in night handovers, a training session on Friday.
Ayesha, who had joined from Lucknow three weeks ago, sat with her notebook open and her pen still. She caught "Friday" and nothing else.
Gautam saw the blank page. He finished his sentence, then said, "Let me repeat in Hindi and English, for Ayesha and anyone else. Three things: new checklist from Monday, handover at the bedside not the station, training Friday at two."
Two other new staff also started writing.
Afterwards, Ayesha found him at the pantry. "Thank you, sir. I was too shy to ask."
"You shouldn't have to ask," Gautam said. "It's your ward too."

qa.q: When is the training session?
qa.a: The training is Friday at two.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling before Gautam repeated the points?
qa.a: Ayesha felt lost and too shy to ask, sitting with her pen still after catching only "Friday".

qa.q: What would you advise a team lead running a meeting like this?
qa.a: Watch for blank pages and still pens, and repeat the key points in a shared language without waiting to be asked.

qa.q: How did the other new staff experience Gautam's repetition?
qa.a: They also felt included and relieved, since they started writing once the points were repeated.

grounding: In a mixed-language hospital meeting, a speaker repeats key points in the shared language so no one is left out.

passage:
Subject: Wednesday's water-sharing meeting
Hi Shankar,
Quick report from Pimpalgaon. The district engineer presented in English, fast, with slides full of terms like "rotation schedule". About forty farmers came; most follow Marathi best, and six seasonal workers from Jharkhand follow only Hindi. After the first slide I saw the back row checking phones.
So I asked the engineer if I could add a line after each point. Short, only the key point: "Mhanje, tumchya shetala pani Mangalvari ani Shukravari yeil," then the same in Hindi.
Phones went down. Bhaskar kaka asked about the Friday slot for the lower fields. One of the Jharkhand workers asked, in Hindi, whether the labourers' quarters were on the same line. The engineer had not thought about that at all.
It added about ten minutes. I'd like to budget for it at every meeting from now on.
Jagdish

qa.q: How many seasonal workers came from Jharkhand?
qa.a: Six seasonal workers from Jharkhand came.

qa.q: What does Jagdish's request to add a line after each point suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Jagdish felt concerned and uneasy that the back row was being left out once the phones came out after the first slide.

qa.q: What small adjustment does Jagdish propose, and why is it worth it?
qa.a: Budgeting about ten minutes at every meeting to repeat key points in Marathi and Hindi, because it brings out questions that would otherwise be missed.

qa.q: What was it like for the Jharkhand workers once the points came in Hindi?
qa.a: They could finally follow and even ask about the labourers' quarters, which made them part of the meeting rather than onlookers.

grounding: Shows a speaker in a mixed-language meeting repeating each key point in Marathi and Hindi so that less fluent listeners are included.
